stories.title: Law Firm Proskauer Rose Expands to 478K SF at SJP’s 11 Times Square
stories.excerpt: Global law firm Proskauer Rose has added roughly 60,000 square feet to its more than 14-story footprint at 11 Times Square. The longtime anchor tenant’s expansion spans floors 31 and 32 of SJP Properties’ 1.1 million square-foot office tower, located at the corner of Eighth Avenue and West 42nd Street one block west of Times Square. The deal brings Proskauer’s total occupancy at 11 Times Square to roughly 478,000 square feet, according to the tenant. The New York Post first reported the deal. Hal Plott, Proskauer’s chief real estate and facilities officer, told Commercial Observer that the coterminous lease renewal and expansion added 15 years to the firm’s current lease, which ended in 2031 and spans 14 and a half stories through the tower’s 30th floor. The deal also secured optionality for significant future expansions. “Given our recent growth, the need for these expansion floors –– and future expansion space beyond those –– was something that was very necessary for us,” Plott told CO. Cushman & Wakefield’s Mark Weiss, Jon Herman and Mike Middleton represented Proskauer, while CBRE’s Paul Amrich negotiated on behalf of SJP. Rent terms were not disclosed, but asking rents in Midtown averaged $95.01 per square foot for direct, Class A office leases in August, according to C&W data. Proskauer relocated to 11 Times Square upon the building’s completion in 2011, taking more than 400,000 square feet at the time. The firm’s newest expansion will be completed in early 2027, according to Plott, when construction is due to wrap up on the 32nd floor. Proskauer’s deal brings 11 Times Square, also known as 640 Eighth Avenue, to a reported occupancy of 93 percent. Other office tenants in the 35-story tower include tech giant Microsoft, global consulting firm Synechron and law firm Rabin Pfeffer and Partners. A spokesperson for C&W declined to comment on the deal. A spokesperson for CBRE did not respond to a request for comment. Emily Davis can be reached edavis@com
bullets: Proskauer Rose expands 60K SF at 11 Times Square, NYC to 478K SF total
15-year lease renewal + coterminous expansion; firm signals growth and long-term NYC commitment
Office demand signal from major tenant; suggests Midtown Manhattan market stabilization
stories.summary: Global law firm Proskauer Rose expanded its footprint at SJP Properties' 11 Times Square in Midtown Manhattan by roughly 60,000 square feet, bringing total occupancy to 478,000 square feet across 14.5+ stories. The deal included a 15-year lease renewal and coterminous expansion of floors 31–32, extending the firm's original 2031 lease termination date while securing future expansion options. The firm cited recent growth as justification for the expansion.
stories.impact: MINIMAL DIRECT RELEVANCE TO MULTIFAMILY. Office tenant expansion signals continued professional-services sector demand in Midtown Manhattan, which supports ancillary residential demand (housing for employees, transient workers), but this is office-driven, not a residential supply or demand shift. Monitor if office resurgence in Midtown fuels housing demand in adjacent submarkets (Hell's Kitchen, Upper West Side).

stories.title: Rockefeller Group Files Plans to Build 340 Apartments at 200 West 97th Street
stories.excerpt: New York City-based developer, owner and operator Rockefeller Group has submitted big housing plans for the Upper West Side development site it bought in January. Rockefeller has filed plans to build a 340-unit, 392,319-square-foot residential building at 200 West 97th Street, according to a recent filing with the New York City Department of Buildings. If approved, the proposed 28-story building would feature 2,465 square feet of ground-floor retail space, as well as a parish center school, a residential lobby and an amenity lounge. The building would have between five and 19 apartment units on each of the second through 28th floors. A terrace and pool are planned for the building’s rooftop. The cellar of the building would also have several amenities, including a pet spa, a podcast room, a screening room, a lounge, a sports simulator and a kids room. The ninth floor would have coworking spaces, a cafe, a fitness center, a “glam room” — though it is unclear exactly what that is — and outdoor space. Timothy Flynn, senior vice president of design and construction for Rockefeller, submitted the plans, while Frank Fusaro from Handel Architects was listed as the architect. Flynn and Fusaro did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. Rockefeller Group and Atlas Capital Group acquired 200 West 97th Street, at the corner of 97th Street and Amsterdam Avenue, in January from the Roman Catholic Church for $96 million, CO reported at the time. As part of the deal, the buyers agreed to preserve the existing church and rectory on the site while redeveloping underutilized parts of the campus into housing. Demolition permits were filed last week for an existing four-story structure on the property. bullets: Rockefeller Group files 340-unit, 28-story residential building at 200 West 97th Street, Manhattan UWS
392K SF with ground-floor retail, parish school, rooftop pool, extensive amenities (pet spa, screening room, coworking)
Entitlement filed; UWS supply pipeline strengthens as major developer accelerates housing

The 28-story building will include 2,465 square feet of ground-floor retail, a parish center/school, residential lobby, rooftop amenities (terrace, pool), and below-grade programming (pet spa, podcast room, screening room, fitness center, sports simulator, kids room). The firm acquired the site in January.
stories.impact: STRONG DEMAND SIGNAL FOR UPPER WEST SIDE. Filing signals confidence in UWS residential demand and Rockefeller's ability to capture it; project adds significant supply (340 units) to a constrained submarket. Concurrent office-to-residential conversions and institutional housing mandates (U of A dorm [#3], Citadel office [#6]) across major metros suggest developers are betting on sustained rental demand. UWS cap rates and land values will reflect increased pipeline visibility; watch for competing deliveries 2027–2029.

stories.title: U of A Breaks Ground on $247M College Dorm
stories.excerpt: As part of its policy to force most first-year students to live on campus, the University of Arizona in Tucson is building a $247 million, on-campus dorm. Called the Catalina, the dorm will house more than 1,300 students in the nine story structure. It is expected to be open to students in the fall of 2028. University of Arizona President Suresh Garimella, added, “Our students who live on campus for at least one year have a 50% higher four-year graduation rate than those who never do.” Developed by Mortenson (MDI) and designed by Gensler, it will include a dining hall, rooftop pool and many other interior and exterior amenities. For the project, Mortenson facilitated a tax-exempt financing structure in partnership with the Collegiate Housing Foundation. Drawing on a national build-to-suit platform and deep expertise in complex projects, MDI partners with public and private stakeholders to deliver thoughtful, long-term real estate solutions that align with each partner’s goals & objectives. The post U of A Breaks Ground on $247M College Dorm appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: University of Arizona breaking ground on $247M on-campus dorm housing 1,300+ students, Tucson
Mortenson/Gensler-developed; opens Fall 2028; tax-exempt financing via Collegiate Housing Foundation

stories.summary: The University of Arizona is building a $247 million, nine-story dormitory called the Catalina in Tucson to house more than 1,300 first-year students. Developed by Mortenson and designed by Gensler, the facility will include a dining hall, rooftop pool, and various interior/exterior amenities. The project is financed through a tax-exempt structure via the Collegiate Housing Foundation and is slated for delivery in Fall 2028. The university's policy mandates most first-year students live on campus, citing a 50% higher four-year graduation rate for on-campus residents.
stories.impact: INSTITUTIONAL SUPPLY SIGNAL FOR TUCSON STUDENT HOUSING. University dorm expansion reduces demand for private purpose-built student housing in Tucson; developers should scrutinize nearby off-campus inventory and capture rates for 2028 forward. However, on-campus mandate + high graduation-rate claim suggest rising enrollment and overall student population growth in Tucson, supporting periphery market development for upper-class housing. Monitor U of A enrollment trends and capital plans for pipeline signals.

stories.title: PGIM Refis Manhattan Office-to-Storage Conversion With $57M Loan
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Mequity Companies and Flatiron Equities Real Estate has sealed a $57 million loan to refinance an office-to-storage conversion project in Midtown Manhattan, Commercial Observer has learned. PGIM supplied the loan for the sponsorship’s transformation of 152 West 36th Street from a 51,853 square-foot Class C office building into a roughly 1,500-unit self-storage facility operated by Manhattan Mini Storage. The refi, which closed Friday afternoon, retires a past construction debt and funds the final development stages of the conversion project, which spans 75,000 rentable square feet and is slated for completion in early 2027. Colliers negotiated the financing with a team led by Dylan Kane, Zach Redding and Jared King. Kane, managing director at Colliers, noted the project is poised for success thanks to a Midtown South rezoning that will boost demand for self-storage in the area because of residential housing that will be sprouting up. The development is slated to receive a temporary certificate occupancy in a few months, according to Kane. “That progress allowed us to increase loan proceeds, lower borrowing costs meaningfully and also provide some runway through the lease-up,” Kane said. Mequity and Flatiron acquired the eight-story office building in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood for $23.8 million from Falcon Properties in September 2024, CO previously reported. The property, originally built as a warehouse, will add eight stories built atop the existing building as part of the conversion. “We’re in a great position to benefit from the new residential demand that will be coming online in the next few years as a result of the Midtown South rezoning,” Mequity CEO Bill Marsh said in a statement. PGIM and Flatiron Equities Real Estate did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: PGIM refinances office-to-storage conversion at 152 West 36th Street, Manhattan Midtown South for $57M
51.8K SF Class C office → 1,500-unit self-storage; completion early 2027
Midtown South rezoning cited as driver of storage demand from incoming residential; adaptive reuse financing appetite evident
stories.summary: A joint venture between Mequity Companies and Flatiron Equities Real Estate secured a $57 million refinance from PGIM for the conversion of a 51,853-square-foot Class C office building at 152 West 36th Street in Midtown South Manhattan into roughly 1,500 self-storage units operated by Manhattan Mini Storage. The refinance retires prior construction debt and funds final development stages; the project spans 75,000 rentable square feet and is scheduled for completion in early 2027. Financing was arranged by Colliers.
stories.impact: INDIRECT DEMAND SIGNAL FOR MANHATTAN RESIDENTIAL. Lender explicitly cited Midtown South rezoning and incoming residential development as a driver of self-storage demand, signaling that new apartment supply in that submarket is expected to materialize and create secondary demand for storage services. This validates pipeline confidence and suggests residential developers should monitor Midtown South rezoning parcels and competitive delivery timelines. Watch for other adaptive reuse financing to accelerate as office-to-residential conversions gain traction.

stories.title: Katy Target to Open Next Month
stories.excerpt: Developer NewQuest announced that a 148,000-square-foot Target store at Texas Heritage Marketplace will open on October 11. It will be one of many popular outlets in the planned 800,000-square-foot retail center. Newquest says it’s investing over $400 million into the center. A Lowe’s and Sam’s Club will join Target as anchor tenants. The Houston Business Journal reports that earlier this year, NewQuest broke ground on the shopping center’s multitenant retail component. It will include 100,021 square feet of junior anchor space, as well as 35,000 square feet of restaurant- and spa- and fitness-related retail, with 5 acres of green space to be called Heritage Grove. The junior anchors include a 51,068-square-foot Academy Sports and Outdoors and 22,147-square-foot Burlington. A 40,000-square-foot EoS Fitness is expected to deliver in the first quarter of 2027. The center is now close to 95% pre-leased. Arch-Con Corp. is the general contractor for multitenant retail construction and site work. AO is the architect. The center will also contain two multifamily communities and a medical office building. The post Katy Target to Open Next Month appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NewQuest opens 148K SF Target at Texas Heritage Marketplace, Katy, Houston; 95% pre-leased retail center
800K SF mixed-use: retail, 2 multifamily, medical office; over $400M invested; two junior anchors + dining/fitness
Retail/multifamily co-development model; Houston demand supports dense, anchor-driven projects
stories.summary: Developer NewQuest is opening a 148,000-square-foot Target store at Texas Heritage Marketplace in Katy, Houston on October 11, anchoring an 800,000-square-foot mixed-use retail center with over $400 million invested. The center includes junior anchors (Academy Sports 51K SF, Burlington 22K SF), restaurants, spa, fitness (EoS Fitness 40K SF, Q1 2027), two multifamily communities, and medical office, plus 5 acres of green space called Heritage Grove. The project is 95% pre-leased.
stories.impact: POSITIVE DEMAND SIGNAL FOR HOUSTON SUBURBS. High pre-leasing (95%) and anchor tenant confidence (Target, Academy Sports) suggest strong retail demand and consumer spending in Katy. Two co-developed multifamily projects within mixed-use center signal developer belief in residential absorption near retail anchors and transit nodes. Monitor Katy submarket rental rates and competing multifamily completions to assess saturation; suburban Houston continues to attract supply capital.

stories.title: Four injured in drill-rig collapse near Citadel HQ development
stories.excerpt: Four people were injured and roads were closed following a drill-rig collapse on Brickell Bay Drive, police say, at the site of billionaire Ken Griffin’s planned Citadel tower. Brickell Bay Drive is closed between Southeast 12th Street and Southeast 13th Street because of the collapse, according to the Miami Police Department. Photos of the scene show the derrick fallen on top of at least two cars. The Monday morning collapse appears to be at Griffin’s 1201 Brickell Bay Drive development site, where he plans a 54-story, 1.7 million square-foot-office building to serve as the headquarters for Citadel and Citadel Securities. bullets: Drill-rig collapse at Citadel HQ site, 1201 Brickell Bay Drive, Miami; 4 injured, 3 cars damaged

The 54-story, 1.7 million-square-foot office tower, developed by Related Companies in partnership with Griffin, is on a 2.5-acre site Griffin purchased for $363 million in 2022. Related stated the incident is under full investigation with city and county cooperation.
stories.impact: MINIMAL DIRECT MULTIFAMILY IMPACT BUT SOFT SIGNAL ON BRICKELL DEVELOPMENT CYCLE. Safety incidents and foundation delays on major office projects can ripple through regional supply chains and labor availability, affecting concurrent multifamily starts in Miami-Dade. Monitor construction timeline revisions; if Citadel project slips, it may ease labor/crane scarcity for competing residential developers in Brickell and Midtown Miami submarkets.

stories.title: PNC Bank Provides $92M Construction Loan for Luxury D.C. Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Carr Properties has secured $92 million of construction debt to build a 299-unit Class A multifamily complex in Downtown Washington, D.C., Commercial Observer can first report. PNC Bank provided the debt, structured with a five-year term and 20-year tax abatement, with United Bank also participating in the deal. Berkadia’s Brian Gould and Pat Cunningham arranged the financing. In a statement, Gould called the development “an especially compelling financing opportunity,” due to the development experience of Carr Properties and rental demand from the affluent D.C. neighborhood of Foggy Bottom and nearby George Washington University. “The project’s 20-year tax abatement further strengthens the economics, and the successful execution of a $92 million construction loan reflects lender confidence in both the sponsorship and the long-term demand for new housing in Foggy Bottom,” added Gould. Located at 2121 Virginia Avenue, the apartment complex will include approximately 16,000 square feet of amenity space, featuring an indoor pool, a club room, a fitness center, coworking spaces, a library, a game room and outdoor courtyards. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first units going on sale in 2028. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: PNC Bank provides $92M construction loan for 299-unit Class A multifamily, Downtown DC (Foggy Bottom)
2121 Virginia Avenue; 5-year term, 20-year tax abatement; strong demand from GWU proximity and affluent neighborhood
Lender confidence in sponsorship (Carr Properties) and market fundamentals; amenity-rich (pool, coworking, fitness, library)
stories.summary: Carr Properties secured a $92 million construction loan from PNC Bank (with United Bank participating) for a 299-unit Class A multifamily complex at 2121 Virginia Avenue in Downtown Washington, D.C.'s Foggy Bottom neighborhood. The loan carries a five-year term and a 20-year tax abatement. The development includes approximately 16,000 square feet of amenity space with an indoor pool, club room, fitness center, coworking spaces, library, game room, and outdoor courtyards. Berkadia arranged the financing.
stories.impact: STRONG CAPITAL AND DEMAND SIGNAL FOR FOGGY BOTTOM/GEORGE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY SUBMARKET. $92M construction loan with 20-year tax abatement reflects lender confidence in Carr Properties' execution and sustained rental demand from GWU-adjacent, affluent neighborhoods. Financing structure validates submarket fundamentals; competitive pressure likely on Class A rents and occupancy. D.C. developers should monitor Foggy Bottom pipeline and cap rate compression from tax abatement plays; tax incentive appetite suggests cap rates compressed, reducing entry cost for institutional sponsors.

stories.title: Malls Rebound to Become Top-Performing U.S. CRE Sector
stories.excerpt: Widely considered an endangered property type following the COVID-19 pandemic, malls are now the top-performing sector in the U.S., the Wall Street Journal reported. Mall values are up 13% over the past year, more than double the increase in overall commercial real-estate prices, the WSJ reported, citing Green Street data. “In terms of how we think about the malls today fundamentally, this is probably the best it’s felt post-Covid,” Ronald Kamdem, head of U.S. REIT and CRE research at Morgan Stanley, told the WSJ. Although lackluster returns in multifamily and office are pushing some investors toward retail and mall properties, malls also have resilient consumer spending and limited retailer bankruptcies in their favor. Shares of Simon Property Group surpassed their previous record high in July for the first time since 2016, and Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield has reconsidered its plans to exit the U.S. mall sector, recently buying out its partners in two West Coast properties. The post Malls Rebound to Become Top-Performing U.S. CRE Sector appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Malls rebound to top-performing US CRE sector; values up 13% YoY vs. 6% overall CRE (Green Street)
Simon Property Group shares hit record highs (first time since 2016); Unibail-Rodamco reconsidering US mall exit
Resilient consumer spending, limited retailer bankruptcies, and investor rotation from weak multifamily/office boost mall demand
stories.summary: According to Green Street data cited by the Wall Street Journal, malls have become the top-performing U.S. commercial real estate sector, with values up 13% over the past year—more than double the 6% increase in overall CRE. Simon Property Group shares surpassed previous record highs in July for the first time since 2016, and Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield has reconsidered its U.S. mall exit, recently acquiring partner stakes in two West Coast properties. Drivers include resilient consumer spending, limited retailer bankruptcies, and investor rotation away from lackluster multifamily and office returns.
stories.impact: INDIRECT COMPETITIVE PRESSURE ON MULTIFAMILY CAPITAL. Mall rebound reflects investor flight from underperforming multifamily (high cap rates, rent growth deceleration) and office (structural vacancy). Capital rotation away from apartments into malls/retail may compress available construction financing for multifamily developers, particularly for non-institutional sponsors. Mixed-use retail + multifamily developments (e.g., Katy project [#5]) may benefit from retail-anchor stability, but standalone multifamily development risk rises as cost of capital increases relative to retail/mall opportunities.

stories.title: Investor Acquires Distressed Atlanta Apartment Asset
stories.excerpt: Liquid Capital Real Estate Investment basically transferred ownership of a Midtown Atlanta apartment complex to Audubon Capital. Audubon picked up the remaining unpaid balance on the loan. The Crest at Midtown property was sold outright rather than a foreclosure. The Atlanta Business Chronicle reported the Liquid Capital affiliates acquired Crest at Midtown for $85.2 million in November 2021. Berkshire Residential Investments extended a $70.9 million loan for the purchase. Developed by Equity Residential and completed in 2001, Crest at Midtown comprises 322 rental units and offers one- and two-bedroom floor plans. It’s located at 215 North Ave., about a mile west of Ponce City Market. Liquid Capital also relinquished ownership of the 212-unit Optimist Lofts community fronting Piedmont Road in Buckhead in 2024. Audubon's acquisition signals continued investor appetite for stabilized, older assets (2001 vintage) at distressed basis. Crest + Optimist combined 534 units indicate concentrated seller pressure; monitor Atlanta Midtown/Buckhead rent trends and cap rate expansion to gauge market stress.

Office tenant expansion at Rockefeller Center reflects continued demand from major financial services employers in Midtown Manhattan, supporting secondary residential demand (housing, turnover, recruitment retention). However, no primary residential supply or demand signal. Monitor if Midtown office stabilization (reflected in Proskauer [#1] and Fifth Third expansions) leads to broader Manhattan residential market upside in adjacent neighborhoods (Hells Kitchen, Upper West Side [#2]).

stories.title: Rich Properties Snags $38.5M Refi for West Palm Beach Rental Asset
stories.excerpt: Rich Properties obtained a $38.55 million refinancing for Tennis Towers Apartments, a 306-unit multifamily community in West Palm Beach that has been owned and operated by Rich Properties for more than 35 years. Berkadia’s Mitch Sinberg, Scott Wadler, Matthew Robbins, Brad Williamson, and Jared Hill arranged the financing on behalf of Rich Properties. Berkadia originated the Freddie Mac-backed, seven-year, fixed-rate loan, which includes four years of interest-only payments.  Built in 1990, Tennis Towers is located at 2882 Tennis Club Drive near Okeechobee Boulevard and I-95. Tennis Towers offers a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom residences ranging from approximately 600 to 1,750 square feet. Community amenities include a tropical swimming pool and sundeck, heated spa, 24-hour fitness center, three tennis courts, BBQ and picnic areas and a car wash area. Tennis Towers provides access to downtown West Palm Beach, CityPlace, Clematis Street and the Brightline station and is approximately 11 minutes from Palm Beach International Airport. The post Rich Properties Snags $38.5M Refi for West Palm Beach Rental Asset appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Rich Properties refinances Tennis Towers Apartments (306 units, West Palm Beach) for $38.55M

Successful refi on stabilized, long-held asset; South Florida multifamily lending remains active despite condo financing tightening

Berkadia originated a Freddie Mac-backed, seven-year, fixed-rate loan with four years of interest-only payments. Built in 1990, Tennis Towers is located at 2882 Tennis Club Drive near Okeechobee Boulevard and I-95, close to downtown West Palm Beach, CityPlace, Clematis Street, and Brightline station.
stories.impact: POSITIVE CAPITAL AVAILABILITY SIGNAL FOR SOUTH FLORIDA MULTIFAMILY. Successful stabilized refi (306 units, 35-year hold) on Freddie Mac platform suggests conventional multifamily financing remains accessible in South Florida despite condo lending tightening ([#12]). Brightline proximity and downtown access support valuations; Tennis Towers refi validates market liquidity for rental properties. Monitor concurrent condo financing strain ([#12]) to assess whether multifamily becomes more attractive relative to condo pre-sales in West Palm Beach submarket.

stories.title: South Florida Dirt: Like pulling teeth: How Fannie, Freddie’s new condo financing rules is affecting deals
stories.excerpt: It’s been a little over a month since Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac tightened the screws on condo lending.  Effective Aug. 3, Fannie Mae retired its limited review process, and Freddie Mac ended its streamlined review process, which allowed lenders to approve conventional mortgages without a deep dive into a condo associations’ finances. All conventional mortgages have to go through the full review process, unless they qualify for a waiver. Projects of 10 units or fewer fall under the waiver qualification.  Forty percent of condos nationwide used the limited review process last year.  And… Florida has the highest concentration of […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac tighten condo financing effective Aug. 3; ended limited/streamlined review processes
40% of US condos used limited review; Florida highest condo concentration; full underwriting now required; non-QM lenders absorb overflow
Deals slower, costlier; mortgage brokers report doubled workload; buyers facing higher non-QM rates if buildings fail thresholds
stories.summary: Effective August 3, Fannie Mae retired its limited review process and Freddie Mac ended its streamlined review process for condo lending. Previously, these processes allowed lenders to approve conventional mortgages without deep dives into condo association finances; now all conventional mortgages must undergo full review unless they qualify for a waiver (projects of 10 units or fewer). Forty percent of U.S. condos used the limited review process last year. Florida, with the highest concentration of condos nationally, is experiencing the most significant impact. Mortgage brokers report deals are slower and costlier, with many buildings failing to meet Fannie or Freddie thresholds, forcing buyers to non-qualified mortgage lenders with higher rates.
stories.impact: CRITICAL CAPITAL IMPACT ON CONDO-HEAVY MARKETS, ESPECIALLY SOUTH FLORIDA. Tightened underwriting shifts buyer financing risk and increases cost of capital for condo purchasers, likely suppressing demand for new condo sales and pre-sale absorption. Developers should pivot to rental (multifamily) product or all-cash syndication models in Florida to avoid condo financing friction. South Florida multifamily rents may benefit from condo-constrained supply; simultaneously, developer financing timelines for condo projects will extend, pushing starts backward and reducing near-term supply competition for rentals.

First phase financed only; full project estimated hundreds of millions to billions; Mayor Lurie commits to faster permitting
25-year entitlement cycle; no full project financing yet; political backing secured but capital model unclear
stories.summary: Irvine-based FivePoint held a groundbreaking ceremony for its 270-acre megadevelopment at the former Candlestick Park site in San Francisco, attended by Rep. Nancy Pelosi, former Speaker Willie Brown, and Mayor Daniel Lurie. The project envisions 7,200 homes, 2.8 million square feet of office and R&D space (innovation district), retail, hospitality, entertainment, and more than 100 acres of parks and open space. Only the first phase (valued at $130 million for infrastructure) is financed; full project completion timelines and financing structures remain unclear.
stories.impact: LONG-CYCLE, UNCERTAIN SUPPLY SIGNAL FOR SAN FRANCISCO BAY AREA. FivePoint's 7,200-unit pipeline is massive for SF metro, but 25-year entitlement and lack of full project financing signal years of phased delivery with uncertain pacing. Political backing (Pelosi, Mayor Lurie) reduces regulatory risk but does not de-risk financing or construction sequencing. Developers should monitor phase-by-phase financing announcements to gauge actual delivery timelines; SF multifamily market may absorb only 200–400 units annually from Candlestick, limiting near-term supply pressure.

bullets: LA County Affordable Housing Solutions Agency issues $220M social bond for 20 affordable housing projects, 1,530 units
Measure A tax revenue funding; grants, construction loans, subordinate notes; 6 acquisitions + renovations; 14 new; 2-3 year delivery
Path Ventures, Linc Housing, Mercy Housing recipients; targeting extremely low and very low-income (ELI/VLI) units
stories.summary: The Los Angeles County Affordable Housing Solutions Agency issued a $220 million social bond to fund 20 affordable housing projects that will create 1,530 units for more than 4,000 residents. Funding supports senior housing, family housing, and housing for people experiencing homelessness. Six projects are acquisitions of existing multifamily properties undergoing renovation; the remaining 14 are new construction expected to complete in two to three years. Developers receiving $1 million to $32 million per project include Path Ventures, Linc Housing, Mercy Housing, the Cesar Chavez Foundation, and West Hollywood Community Housing Corporation. Most units target extremely low-income (ELI) and very low-income (VLI) households.
stories.impact: SUPPLY PIPELINE SIGNAL FOR LOS ANGELES AFFORDABLE HOUSING. $220M Measure A-funded program adds 1,530 units to LA pipeline with 2–3 year delivery horizon; significantly addresses ELI/VLI shortfall cited by LACAHSA. Acquisition + renovation strategy (6 projects) removes stabilized properties from market-rate pool, moderately constraining Class B/C supply. Market-rate developers should monitor acquisition activity and price pressure; tax-subsidized affordable projects set below-market comp pricing, potentially anchoring rents downward in targeted submarkets (Inglewood, Long Beach, Downey, Claremont). Watch for interaction with private Class A development (e.g., Rockefeller's UWS project [#2]) to assess tenant stratification and income targeting.

bullets: SpaceX sues Ken Paxton, Grimes County over Terafab planning/tax incentive records release; $55B semiconductor plant
100M SF vertically integrated chip fab, 15 miles from College Station, Texas; joint SpaceX/xAI venture; construction imminent
Musk litigation blocks transparency; massive employer anchors regional infrastructure and housing demand near College Station
stories.summary: SpaceX filed a lawsuit against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's office and Grimes County to block the release of confidential planning and tax incentive records related to Terafab, a $55 billion, 100-million-square-foot semiconductor manufacturing facility located approximately 15 miles from College Station, Texas. The plant is a joint venture between SpaceX and xAI and is set to begin construction. The litigation was triggered by public records requests from two county residents seeking information on tax incentives negotiated between the county and Terafab sponsors.
stories.impact: MAJOR DEMAND ANCHOR FOR COLLEGE STATION/GRIMES COUNTY REGION. Terafab's $55B investment and 100M SF footprint represents one of the largest industrial anchors in Texas; massive job creation (thousands of construction + permanent roles) will drive in-migration to College Station, Bryan, and surrounding counties over 3–5 years. Developers should immediately acquire land and underwrite multifamily/industrial projects within 10–20 miles of the Terafab site (near I-45 corridor). Rents and valuations will appreciate 2025–2027 as workforce relocates. Monitor tax incentive transparency litigation for clues on project timeline and phase-in; state/county incentive structures will influence cost basis and financing returns for regional developers.

stories.title: Patriot Equities plots redevelopment of Atlantic City racetrack
stories.excerpt: A long-shuttered horse racing track with ties to Bob Hope and Frank Sinatra appears destined for a development refresh, thanks in part to the arrival of an Amazon warehouse. Wayne-based Patriot Equities purchased a 110-acre section of the Atlantic City Race Course in Mays Landing from Greenwood ACRA, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported. The price of the parcel was not disclosed; Greenwood paid $13 million for the entire 255-acre property in 2001, envisioning an off-track betting facility that was never built. The larger 145-acre portion of the property that didn’t go to Patriot was sold instead to Amazon, which is […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Patriot Equities acquires 110 acres of Atlantic City Race Course site, Mays Landing, NJ; Amazon warehouse adjacent
Former horse-racing track (built 1946, closed 2015); Amazon 1.2M SF warehouse + PILOT agreement; Patriot planning mixed-use commercial/residential
110 acres zoned residential; Amazon adjacency signals supply/logistics demand; redevelopment feasibility hinges on commercial zoning/approvals
stories.summary: Wayne-based Patriot Equities purchased 110 acres of the 255-acre Atlantic City Race Course site in Mays Landing from Greenwood ACRA. The remaining 145 acres were sold to Amazon for a 1.2-million-square-foot warehouse with a PILOT agreement. Patriot is planning a mixed-use development with commercial and residential components on property currently zoned for residential use. The historic racetrack, built in 1946 with ties to Bob Hope and Frank Sinatra, closed in 2015 and has been vacant ever since.
stories.impact: LOGISTICS-ANCHORED MIXED-USE OPPORTUNITY IN SOUTH JERSEY. Amazon's 1.2M SF warehouse validates supply chain demand for South Jersey/Philadelphia exurban corridor; Patriot's adjacent 110-acre mixed-use site (commercial + residential) can capture warehouse worker and regional demand. Zoning shift from residential to commercial required; if approved, site is positioned for logistics-workforce housing, light industrial, and retail. Monitor PILOT agreement terms to assess tax burden on Patriot; watch Mays Landing municipal approvals to gauge development feasibility. Philadelphia-area developers should monitor larger site repositioning (former industrial/entertainment → e-commerce ecosystems) for pipeline signals.
